title: Beijing Is Celebrating a Race It Never Ran
gist: Pew's 2026 global survey shows China viewed more favorably than the United States in 25 of 36 countries and more confidence in Xi than Trump in 22 — an unprecedented result since Pew began asking in 2002 — but the author argues the shift is entirely a US collapse rather than a Chinese soft-power win. China's favorability correlates inversely with per capita GDP and China is named the top threat by 76% of Filipinos, 53% of Japanese and 52% of Australians, so under Nye's definition (attraction, not payment) the gains do not qualify as soft power and are reversible via the 'soft power pendulum'.

themes.theme: Headline numbers vs. the actual Pew data

insights.claim: Pew's 2026 survey found China viewed more favorably than the United States in 25 of 36 countries and regions, with more confidence expressed in Xi Jinping than Donald Trump in 22 — results Pew has never produced since it began asking the question in 2002.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: A genuine regime break in global opinion that will be cited to justify allied hedging and de-dollarisation arguments regardless of its cause.
insights.locator: There is no gainsaying the fact that the headline findings are startling

insights.claim: The Global Times editorial claiming 27 of 36 countries 'chose China' overcounted: the real number is 25, with two of the claimed countries showing gaps too small to be meaningful.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Chinese state-media framing of Western survey data inflates margins; verify against the underlying report before trading the narrative.
insights.quote: Actually, the number is 25. The other two are countries where the gap is too small to mean anything. The editorial writer counted them anyway.
insights.locator: The Global Times could not help itself

insights.claim: The United States still leads China on favorability in only six countries — India, Israel, Japan, the Philippines, Poland and South Korea — and neither Canada nor Mexico is among them.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: The remaining pro-US bloc maps almost exactly onto states with a direct China security threat — a usable map of which alliances hold under stress.
insights.locator: The United States leads in six

insights.claim: China's median favorability across the 37 countries surveyed is 51% against 39% unfavorable, a materially positive absolute reading rather than merely a relative win.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Even discounting the US collapse, China's absolute standing gives Beijing real room to recruit partners for trade and standards blocs.
insights.quote: China's median favorability across 37 countries is 51 percent against 39 unfavorable, which is nothing to sneeze at
insights.locator: On the other hand, China's median favorability

themes.theme: Money buys affection, power buys fear

insights.claim: Plotting China's favorability against per capita GDP produces a downward-sloping line: China scores best in the countries where it lends, builds and buys, which disqualifies the result as soft power under Joseph Nye's definition excluding coercion or payment.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Chinese goodwill is a purchased asset that decays if lending slows — track Chinese outbound credit as the leading indicator of its favorability numbers.
insights.quote: China does best where it lends, builds, and buys. Nye's payment clause disqualifies that as soft power.
insights.locator: Consider where China's numbers are strong

insights.claim: Three-quarters or more of respondents view China favorably in Indonesia, Kenya, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, while seven in ten or more view it unfavorably in Israel, Japan, South Korea, Sweden and the United States.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: The favorability split is a near-perfect proxy for who is a net recipient of Chinese capital versus a net rival — useful for mapping market-access risk.
insights.locator: Per Pew's breakdown, three-quarters or more respondents

insights.claim: In an open-ended question naming the greatest threat to their own country, 76% of Filipinos, 53% of Japanese and 52% of Australians named China, while respondents in Bangladesh, Indonesia, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Thailand ranked China as less of a threat than the United States.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: This is the buried finding: proximity to Chinese hard power flips sentiment, so favorability data cannot be read as willingness to align.
insights.quote: China is welcome wherever it arrives with money and feared wherever it arrives with power.
insights.locator: Pew asked people, with no list in an open-ended question

insights.claim: Only in 11 of 37 countries do around half or more respondents say the Chinese government respects its people's personal freedoms, and roughly three-quarters or more say it does not across North America, nearly all of Europe, Australia, Japan and South Korea.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Underlying perceptions of Chinese governance have not improved, so the favorability gain is thin and will not survive a US recovery.
insights.quote: So people haven't really changed their opinion of what China is.
insights.locator: Now drill down into those numbers further

insights.claim: Pakistan is the standout at 90% favorable toward China — the highest of any country Pew surveyed — with three-quarters naming China their top ally, explained by the absence of a China border dispute and Pakistan's use of China as a hedge against India.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: The one neighbour with no territorial quarrel with Beijing is its most favorable — territorial disputes, not ideology, drive regional sentiment.
insights.locator: Pakistan is an interesting exception

insights.claim: Thailand is one of very few countries where China's favorability actually fell — by 11 points — while Thai concern about Chinese territorial conduct rose from 38% in 2024 to 52% in 2026.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Thailand is the early-warning case for Southeast Asian sentiment reversal on Beijing; watch Bangkok policy for hedging moves.
insights.locator: The numbers from Thailand, too, merit closer inspection

themes.theme: The scale of the US reputational collapse

insights.claim: The share of Canadians viewing the United States as a reliable partner fell from 83% in 2022 to 35% in 2026, a 48-point collapse in the view of America's closest neighbour.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Canadian trust destruction of this magnitude has direct read-through to USMCA renegotiation, defence procurement and cross-border investment flows.
insights.quote: In 2022, 83 percent of Canadians viewed the United States as a reliable partner; today, it is 35 percent.
insights.locator: Now to reckon with the American side of the report

insights.claim: Only 23% of Germans now say Washington considers the interests of countries like theirs, down from 60% three years earlier and a more negative reading than during the Iraq War.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: German opinion below Iraq War lows underpins the European strategic-autonomy and defence-spending trade.
insights.quote: a more negative reading than during the Iraq War
insights.locator: Ask Germans whether Washington considers the interests

insights.claim: Favorable views of the United States fell significantly in 15 of the 24 countries with year-on-year data, and confidence in Trump dropped in 16 of 24 while rising in none.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Zero countries improved their view of Trump — an unambiguous directional signal for US diplomatic leverage in trade and alliance talks.
insights.quote: Confidence in Trump dropped in 16 of 24 and rose in none.
insights.locator: Favorable views of the United States fell significantly

insights.claim: Pew's fieldwork ran from 8 February to 13 May 2026, straddling the war with Iran, and its own regression analysis found opinion of the United States sinking week by week as the fieldwork progressed.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: The result is event-driven and still deteriorating within the sample window, meaning the true current level may be worse than published.
insights.quote: its own regression analysis found opinion of the United States sinking week by week as the fieldwork rolled on
insights.locator: Pew was in the field from Feb. 8 to May 13

insights.claim: Favorable views of China reached 51% in Italy, up 20 points since 2022 and the first time in nearly two decades of polling that half of Italians looked kindly on China, while Spain at 54% is net positive for the first time since 2011.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Southern Europe is the soft flank for EU China policy — watch Rome and Madrid for divergence on screening, 5G and EV tariffs.
insights.locator: In Italy, favorable views of China sit at 51 percent

insights.claim: China has overtaken the United States not through its own efforts but as a result of a US collapse, and in a year when China did nothing new — so Beijing cannot claim agency for the result.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Positioning that assumes durable Chinese soft-power gains is mispriced; the driver is exogenous and reverses with US politics.
insights.quote: A survey in which China's numbers improved during a year when it did nothing new should be cause for reflection in Beijing, rather than celebration.
insights.locator: A closer reading of the Pew report shows

insights.claim: US standing has cratered before — in 2008 as Bush left office and in 2017 as Trump arrived — but Pew researcher Jonathan Schulman told the BBC that even at those lows favorable views of China ran level with America's or slightly behind, which makes 2026 a genuine departure.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: This is the first cycle where a US slump translated into a Chinese lead — the structural change is that China now absorbs the spillover.
insights.locator: The U.S. standing has cratered before

insights.claim: Hendrik Ohnesorge's 'soft power pendulum' framework holds that US global approval has swung with every US election for three decades, citing German approval hitting historic lows under Bush and recovering almost overnight when Obama took office.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Reputational mean reversion is fast and election-triggered; the 2028 US election is the natural catalyst date for a snapback.
insights.quote: calls it the "soft power pendulum." It has swung with every U.S. election for three decades
insights.locator: And collapses, even on this scale, can be reversed

insights.claim: Gallup independently found China overtaking the United States in global approval last year by the widest margin in almost 20 years, but read the preference as reflecting 'deep negativity toward the U.S. more than strong enthusiasm for China'.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Two independent pollsters converge on the same causal reading — the signal is US-driven, corroborating the reversibility case.
insights.quote: deep negativity toward the U.S. more than strong enthusiasm for China
insights.locator: That Global Times editorial, as it happens, cited Gallup

insights.claim: The Asia Society Policy Institute's own annual survey of global opinion on China finds Beijing's standing has only recovered slightly from its pandemic-era slump, contradicting claims of a soft-power breakthrough.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Third data source undercutting the China-wins narrative; use it to fade momentum trades built on the Pew headline.
insights.locator: The Asia Society Policy Institute, running its own annual survey

insights.claim: Research suggests expressions of pro-China sentiment often serve as a way for global audiences to register anger at the United States rather than as genuine preference for China.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Treat pro-China polling as a protest vote proxy; it will not translate into commitments Beijing can bank.
insights.locator: What Beijing cannot claim is agency

insights.claim: Joseph Nye coined 'soft power' in Foreign Policy 36 years ago and defined it as getting the outcomes you want through attraction rather than coercion or payment, a clause commentators covering the Pew result systematically dropped.
insights.speaker: Bobby Ghosh
insights.so_what: Definitional discipline is the edge here: most coverage, including Bloomberg's, mislabelled paid influence as soft power.
insights.quote: Soft power, he said, is the ability to get the outcomes you want through attraction rather than coercion or payment.
insights.locator: But before we get to that, it's useful to revisit the definition
